result.abstractText: This case highlights a critical but easily overlooked complication of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) management-iatrogenic hyperchloremic acidosis superimposed on ketoacidosis-and demonstrates the role of the Δ gap (ΔAG - ΔHCO3 -) in identifying refractory mixed acidosis. The "peripheral metabolic pool" hypothesis is proposed as a possible additional mechanism for persistent pH deterioration despite improvement in central metabolic parameters. A 32-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes presented with severe DKA (pH 6.974) after excessive durian and beer consumption. Despite initial improvement in glucose and ketone levels, her pH paradoxically worsened to 6.84 with progressive hyperchloremia (96.8 to 115 mmol/L), leading to acute heart failure, acute kidney injury, among others. The Δ gap=ΔAG-ΔHCO3 -<-6 suggested the possible coexistence of high anion-gap ketoacidosis and normal anion-gap hyperchloremic acidosis, consistent with a mixed acidosis. Urinary β2-microglobulin >4000 μg/L indicated proximal tubular injury. Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) was initiated at 14 hours after admission; acidosis was successfully corrected after 12 hours of CRRT, with gradual recovery of organ function. Recognition of mixed acidosis and timely individualized CRRT were important in breaking this patient's vicious cycle. Clinicians should avoid excessive chloride load in DKA management and consider balanced crystalloids after initial resuscitation.

result.title: Recurrent Euglycemic Diabetic Ketoacidosis Weeks After SGLT2 Inhibitor Cessation: A Case Report.
result.authorString: Mansour C, Katrib E, Mansour M, Fares M.

result.abstractText: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis (EDKA) is a complication of sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors that is being increasingly documented. It is challenging to diagnose, especially in critically ill patients because hyperglycemia is absent or mild. We report the case of a 71-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus previously treated with dapagliflozin, which had been discontinued 2 weeks before presentation, who was admitted for tracheostomy and percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) placement in the context of a neurodegenerative disorder. On postoperative day 2, he was transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU) for aspiration pneumonia complicated by septic shock. He subsequently experienced recurrent episodes of high anion gap metabolic acidosis associated with positive ketonuria and relative euglycemia. The initial episode was interpreted as mixed septic lactic acidosis and SGLT2 inhibitor-associated EDKA, whereas later episodes were more consistent with isolated recurrent EDKA. Management consisted of treatment of the underlying septic shock, and repeated courses of fixed intravenous (IV) insulin infusions to close the anion gap while maintaining euglycemia. This case demonstrates the importance of suspecting EDKA, especially in critically ill patients on SGLT2 inhibitors who present with unexplained high anion gap metabolic acidosis, even when lactic acidosis is present. Early diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent complications and relapse.
